title: A flood in Nepal leaves hundreds dead or missing - Materia Rinnovabile | Renewable Matter
description: A flood in Nepal leaves hundreds dead or missing  Materia Rinnovabile | Renewable Matter
publisher.title: Materia Rinnovabile | Renewable Matter
full_article:
An enormous mass of debris, water and mud swept away buildings, roads, bridges and hundreds of people within moments, many of whom are still missing. Terrifying images are emerging from Nepal, where, on Wednesday 26 August, a flash flood struck Rasuwa District, on the border with China’s Tibet Autonomous Region. As of 8 p.m. CEST, the confirmed death toll stood at 98, according to Reuters , citing local police. Among those missing are numerous tourists of different nationalities.

Several hours after the event, as rescue operations continue, the precise circumstances that triggered one of the most serious disasters in the Himalayan region in recent years remain unclear. However, initial analyses of satellite imagery indicate that the event may have been caused by a glacier collapse. The collapse of part of the glacier is thought to have sent a mass of ice, rocks, water and sediment down into the valley, triggering the flood.

According to local authorities, there is still a risk of a further collapse, while rescue and evacuation operations have been made more difficult by the destruction of roads and infrastructure.

The glacier collapse and the formation of the flood

Satellite images taken by Planet Labs before and after the event and analysed by Reuters show a dramatic change in the landscape: an area of mountain slopes previously covered in vegetation is now buried beneath debris and sediment.

According to Vikram Gupta, an engineering geology specialist and lecturer at Sikkim University in India, who was interviewed by Reuters , “It’s confirmed that a substantial portion of that glacier snout collapsed to initiate the event – ​probably including or entraining a fair amount of rock and sediment”.

The collapse is believed to have generated a large avalanche of ice and rocky material, which swept down towards the valley floor. Along its path, the mass may have mobilised additional sediment and interfered with the course of the Lhende Khola, contributing to the flood, which then rapidly propagated along the valley.

The exact dynamics are still being analysed, but satellite imagery represents one of the most important elements in reconstructing the event. Comparing images taken before and after the disaster makes it possible to identify the area from which part of the glacier is thought to have detached, as well as the path taken by the debris as it moved downstream.

The risk of a natural dam

What is now causing concern, however, is an accumulation of debris upstream that continues to obstruct the Lhende Khola, creating the risk of another flood. When a landslide, rock avalanche or mass of ice temporarily blocks a river, water can accumulate behind the natural dam. If the barrier subsequently fails, even partially, the sudden release of water can generate another flood wave, capable of carrying sediment and debris throughout the valley.

For this reason, Nepal’s authorities have evacuated the area and urged communities living along the river to remain alert, while India has issued flood warnings for the states of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, which are crossed by several rivers flowing from the Himalayas towards the plains.

Meanwhile, India has sent 10 tonnes of aid, while the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies has allocated one million Swiss francs through its Disaster Response Emergency Fund to support the Nepal Red Cross. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, expressing her solidarity with those affected by the disaster, announced the activation of Copernicus to help map the affected areas and support the response, while also making further assistance available.

Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah urged the country to remain united. “The pain and loss you have suffered is not small. But I want to assure you that you are not alone in this difficult time – the state is with you with all its means and resources,” Shah said in a statement posted to social media. “Please be patient. The government takes full responsibility for your rescue, treatment, food and shelter. In times of such a disaster, we all need to stand together.”

title: Wall of floodwater sweeps away villages in Nepal, hundreds missing - Scientific American
description: Wall of floodwater sweeps away villages in Nepal, hundreds missing  Scientific American
publisher.title: Scientific American
full_article:
A huge flood, thought to be triggered when a large chunk of ice broke off a high mountain glacier, has swept through settlements in Nepal and Tibet, an autonomous region of China. The waters—seen with people trying to run away on surveillance footage—crashed through buildings. And they have killed at least 160 people, with hundreds more missing, including foreign tourists, according to officials in Nepal and China.

Daniel Shugar, a geologist at the University of Calgary in Alberta, found satellite imagery that appears to show a chunk of glacier about 2,000 feet wide that broke off and caused what is called an ice avalanche as it dropped almost 4,000 feet. “The bottom looks like a bomb exploded—it’s just deposits from the broken-up glacier,” he told the New York Times. The flow of the pulverized ice moved down a valley toward the Bhotekoshi River at the border between Nepal and Tibet.

Houses in Nuwakot on August 26. RANABHAT/AFP/Getty Images

A similar event happened in India in 2021, destroying a hydroelectric dam project and killing 42 people.

The role of global warming in destabilizing the glacier still needs to be investigated, but glaciers in the Himalayas, as everywhere, have seen significant melt and retreat. This decrease is causing some glaciers to destabilize, along with cliffs they once buttressed. It is also causing sudden outbursts of glacial lakes. More than a third of the glacial ice in the region could disappear by the end of the century, according to some estimates, taking with it a crucial source of water for hundreds of millions of people.

Rescue personnel use an excavator to carry a person affected by flash floods at Devghat in Nuwakot on August 26. Prakash MATHEMA/AFP/Getty Images

There could be other contributing factors to the flooding as well, Shugar said, because overcast conditions have hampered satellite analysis.

Nepal’s army is carrying out search-and-rescue operations.

title: In Nepal Floods, Glacial Lake Link And Flashback To Last Year's Tragedy - NDTV
description: In Nepal Floods, Glacial Lake Link And Flashback To Last Year's Tragedy  NDTV
publisher.title: NDTV
full_article:
An avalanche of ice and rock, likely a result of glacial lake outburst, triggered massive flash floods that tore through parts of Nepal, killing at least 95 people and causing extensive damage to villages and infrastructure.

Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development say an avalanche from a glacier likely caused Wednesday's flash flood.

The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River, witnessed maximum flooding, experts said.

"The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in fourteen months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream," Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group, told news agency AFP.

"In a warming Himalaya, early warning is the first line of adaptation," he added.

The worst affected area, Rasuwa district, witnessed similar flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in neighboring Tibet overflowed as a result of high temperatures in the mountain region. Nine people lost their lives and critical infrastructure including a bridge connecting the two countries were damaged at the time.

An aerial view of the houses partially submerged in mud-laden flash flood following an outburst in the Bhotekoshi River, in Nepal's Rasuwa on Wednesday

The Himalayan region, which crosses Nepal and several nearby countries including India, is especially vulnerable to heavy rains, floods and landslides because the area is warming up faster than the rest of the world due to human-caused climate change. Research has shown that extreme weather events including heat waves, heavy rains and melting glaciers have become more frequent in the region.

Researchers at the Kathmandu research group found earlier this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting at an accelerating rate, with ice loss rates doubling since 2000 primarily due to rising global temperatures and climate change.

Monsoon rains from June to September regularly trigger deadly floods and landslides across South Asia. Scientists say climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events in the region.

Officials said 384 tourists, including 291 from countries including India, the United States, the United Kingdom and Malaysia, were reported missing as a result of today's flash flood.

The Bhotekoshi River flooded around 9 am, destroying several villages as well as roads and hydropower projects, officials said. They issued warnings to residents of several of Nepal's districts and asked them to stay away from the banks of Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.

In this screengrab from a video, floodwater flows across a residential area in Nepal

Videos shared by Nepal Police and others on social media showed torrents of muddy water crashing through mountain valleys in the landlocked country.

The Nepal Army said it had deployed helicopters and disaster response personnel to the affected area.

The Nepal Electricity Authority said about 430 megawatts of production capacity, including from hydropower and solar facilities, has been damaged. Several highways were also closed, Nepalese authorities said.

title: Deadly flash flood wipes away villages in Nepal, Tibet - dw.com
description: Deadly flash flood wipes away villages in Nepal, Tibet  dw.com
publisher.title: dw.com
full_article:
Dozens of people were confirmed dead and hundreds more are missing after a flash flood swept through remote valleys in Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday.

Nepali police said that authorities have recovered 157 bodies. Officers were "working to move families in flood-risk areas... to safer locations," police said.

"The pain and loss you have suffered is not small. But I want to assure you that you are not alone in this difficult time -- the state is with you with all its means and resources," Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a statement posted to social media. "Please be patient. The government takes full responsibility for your rescue, treatment, food and shelter. In times of such a disaster, we all need to stand together."

In China, authorities said at least three have died, with 265 still missing, China's state broadcaster CCTV ‌said

The floodwaters washed away villages, damaged bridges and destroyed electrical infrastructure on both sides of the Nepal-China border.

"There is devastation everywhere we look," ‌Tula ​Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa district, told Reuters.

"The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing."

At the same time, Chinese authorities also reported that a mudslide caused "major casualties" on the other side of the border in Tibet.

Security cameras captured the moment a wall of mud hit the Nepal-China border Image: REUTERS

Hundreds of people missing

Nepal's Tourism Ministry said 403 travelers were reported missing for several hours after the floods struck.

Missing travelers included 341 foreign tourists, among them 142 Indians. Other nationalities of those missing included people from Australia, Britain, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa, South Korea and the United States, the tourism board said.

A Nepali police spokesperson told Germany's DPA news agency that dozens of personnel were also missing.

"So far, we only have confirmation of 26 police personnel who remain missing in the flood," they said.

"We also have missing information of government revenue officials, hydropower workers among others. But we are still collecting the data."

Villages in Rasuwa district were swept away by the deluge of water and mud Image: Sunil Sharma/ZUMA/IMAGO

What caused the flash floods?

Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said an earthquake triggered an avalanche in the Himalayas that then triggered flash floods in the valleys below.

Chinese state news agency Xinhua said a mudslide on the Nepali side of the mountains spread to Gyirong County in Tibet.

"Entire villages and market areas have been wiped out," said David Fisher, the Nepal head of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).

The burst river also inundated villages in Dhading district Image: REUTERS

Major rescue operations underway

Nepal dispatched more than a dozen rescue helicopters to the mountainous Rasuwa region, but floodwaters were too high for the helicopters to land.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the military and police were assisting with rescues.

"Instructions have been given ... to move ​the people living in the lower areas ⁠to safer places," he said. "People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert."

Chinese President Xi Jinping also ordered an "all out" rescue effort.

He said "the most urgent task is doing everything possible to search for and rescue the missing people... quickly treat injured people and minimize casualties to the greatest extent possible," according to Chinese state media.

Rescue helocopters were initually unable to land due to the high floodwaters Image: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP

A second flood may be imminent, according to Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.

"With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur," he told the AFP news agency.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

बाढ़िक पानि नेपाल-चीन सीमाक दुनू कात गाम-गाम बहल, पुल क्षतिग्रस्त आ विद्युत आधारभूत संरचना नष्ट भ गेल।

रसुवा जिला के स्वास्थ्यकर्मी तुला बहादुर बीके रायटर के कहलनि जे, जतय देखैत छी तबाही भ रहल अछि।

सैकड़ों लोग लापता

नेपालके पर्यटन मन्त्रालयके कहब अछि जे बाढिक बाद कतेको घंटासँ ४०३ यात्री लापता हेबाक सूचना भेटल अछि ।

लापता यात्री मे 341 विदेशी पर्यटक शामिल छलाह, जाहि मे 142 भारतीय शामिल छथि। पर्यटन बोर्ड के कहब अछि जे लापता लोक के अन्य राष्ट्रीयता मे ऑस्ट्रेलिया, ब्रिटेन, मलेशिया, नीदरलैंड, पुर्तगाल, दक्षिण अफ्रीका, दक्षिण कोरिया आ अमेरिका के लोक शामिल अछि।

नेपाली पुलिस प्रवक्ता जर्मनीक डीपीए समाचार एजेन्सी के कहलनि जे, दर्जनों जवान सेहो लापता अछि।

ओ सब कहलनि जे, एखन धरि हमरा सब लग मात्र 26 पुलिसकर्मी के पुष्टि अछि जे बाढ़ि मे लापता अछि।

फ्लैश फ्लड के कारण की भेल?

नेपाल के विदेश मंत्री शिसिर खनाल कहलनि जे, हिमालय मे भूकंप सं हिमस्खलन भेल जे फेर नीचा घाटी मे आकस्मिक बाढ़ि शुरू भ गेल।

चीन के सरकारी समाचार एजेंसी सिन्हुआ के कहनाय छनि जे पहाड़ के नेपाली तरफ के कीचड़ के झटका तिब्बत के ग्यारोंग काउंटी तक फैलल अछि.

अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय रेडक्रस आ रेड क्रिसेंट सोसाइटी फेडरेशन (आईएफआरसी)के नेपाल प्रमुख डेविड फिशर कहलनि जे, सम्पूर्ण गाम आ बजार क्षेत्र सफाया कएल गेल अछि ।

प्रमुख बचाव कार्य चलि रहल अछि

नेपाल एक दर्जन स बेसी बचाव हेलीकॉप्टर कए पहाड़ी रसुवा क्षेत्र पठेलक, मुदा बाढ़िक पानि बहुत बेसी छल जाहि स हेलीकॉप्टर उतरबा लेल नहि आबि सकल।

नेपाली प्रधानमन्त्री बलेन्द्र शाह सेना आ प्रहरी उद्धारमे सहयोग कऽ रहल बतौलनि ।

ओ कहलनि जे, निर्देश देल गेल अछि ... निचला इलाका मे रहय वाला लोक के ⁠सुरक्षित जगह पर ल जेबाक लेल। "नदी के किनारे के लोक के सलाह देल गेल अछि जे ओ अतिरिक्त सावधानी बरतथि आ सतर्क रहथि।"

चीन के राष्ट्रपति शी जिनपिंग न॑ भी “ऑल आउट” बचाव प्रयास के आदेश देलकै ।

चीनी सरकारी मीडिया के अनुसार, हुनी कहलकै कि सबसें जरूरी काम छै कि लापता लोगऽ के खोज आरू बचाबै लेली हर संभव प्रयास करलऽ जाय... घायल लोगऽ के जल्दी स॑ इलाज करलऽ जाय आरू सबसें जादा नुकसान कम स॑ कम करलऽ जाय ।

बाढ़ के अधिक पानी के कारण बचाव हेलोकॉप्टर शुरू में उतरय में असमर्थ छल छवि : प्रबिन रानाभाट/एएफपी

इंटरनेशनल सेंटर फॉर इंटीग्रेटेड माउंटेन डेवलपमेंट केरऽ जलवायु आरू पर्यावरणीय जोखिम केरऽ प्रमुख किआंगगोंग झांग के अनुसार दोसरऽ बाढ़ आसन्न होय सकै छै ।

ओ एएफपी समाचार एजेंसी केँ कहलनि जे, नेपाल-चीन सीमावर्ती नदी पर एखनो अपस्ट्रीम मे रुकावट पड़ल अछि, अधिकारी सब चेतावनी दैत छथि जे दोसर बाढ़ि आबि सकैत अछि।

The yellow star marks the location of the landslide and glacier collapse, according to the USGS. The Nepal flash flood that followed swept away entire villages. The true death toll is unknown at this time. Image via USGS.

Nepal flash flood wipes out villages after glacier collapse

On August 26, 2026, a massive flash flood stormed down river valleys in Nepal. While there was initial confusion about what caused the event, it now appears that a glacier collapse triggered a landslide and the flash flood that wiped away villages downstream. According to the USGS, the landslide from the collapse registered as 5.2 on the Richter scale on local seismometers. It occurred at 2:52:10 UTC, which would have been 8:37 a.m. Nepal time, which is 5 hours and 45 minutes ahead of Universal Coordinated Time. The location was near the border of Nepal and China, about 34 miles (55 km) northwest of Kodari, Nepal.

Initially, it was believed that a earthquake triggered the collapse. But the USGS said:

This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake. Additional analysis of long period seismic waves indicate that the seismic energy was instead generated by a landslide. The location of this event was estimated from satellite images.

Flash floods due to a glacier collapse and landslide

Dave Petley, who writes the landslide blog at EOS (a news magazine of the American Geophysical Union), is a world leader in the study and management of landslides. He explained what we know about the event so far at EOS:

The catastrophic debris flow that struck Nepal and Tibet today was triggered by the collapse of a glacier high in the mountains. … The root cause of this disaster is already known, although there is a lot of misinformation and some uncertainty. … There has been some speculation, and indeed official comments, that the trigger was an earthquake. This is likely to be a misinterpretation of the data – the seismic signal is almost certainly the rock ice avalanche and debris flow, not a tectonic event.

So it appears that a glacier collapse was the trigger for the floods. Why that glacier collapsed, due to global warming or something else, is not immediately clear. But Petley does speculate about how a glacier collapse could turn into liquid water so quickly:

A fascinating element of this is the source of the huge volume of water. This may be a combination of ice that converted to water as a result of the release of energy from the initial collapse, water embedded in the sediments that were entrained en route and river water. But I am speculating. There is no evidence that this was a glacial lake outburst flood. Understanding this event is going to need an international team, as has been the case for similar events in recent years. That team has now got together and has started work.

Below is a before-and-after view of where the glacier collapsed.

Nepal flash flood videos from social media

Please be warned that these videos contain images that you can’t unsee. It is clear from the videos that many in the path of the flood had no chance to escape.

The first video is from the Nepal-Tibet border crossing at Gyirong Port.

Flash flood kills many on Nepal-China border 0:57 • Source: CNN Flash flood kills many on Nepal-China border 0:57

Flash floods in Nepal and a mudslide in Tibet have caused widespread devastation, with hundreds missing after floodwater swept through riverside settlements in the north of Nepal, leaving destruction in its wake.

At least 95 people have died in the disaster, Nepali police said earlier today, but that toll is expected to rise once the waters recede and the true extent of the damage becomes clear. Three people have been killed in Tibet and 265 others are missing, Chinese authorities just reported.

Here’s what we know.

What caused the flooding?

At 8:37 a.m. local time, a 4.4 magnitude earthquake was reported by US Geological Survey to have struck along the Nepal-China border, north of Kathmandu.

Around the same time, an “avalanche” of ice and rock — more like a landslide in this case — tore down a mountainside and into the Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi River, which flows from China into Nepal, often through deep gorges.

Whether the quake triggered a landslide, or the earthquake-like shaking was caused by the landslide itself, is still being investigated, but a group of scientists investigating the causes believes it was the latter.

This landslide likely “released a sudden surge downstream,” said Saswata Sanyal, of the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development in Kathmandu, a regional climate organization.

What’s the impact been?

Videos have shown the devastation unleashed by the powerful floodwaters which swept off the mountains. A major land border crossing between China and Nepal was completely overwhelmed in less than a minute, with a mudslide appearing to wipe out everything in its path, engulfing those trying to flee.

Elsewhere, footage shows torrential flood water tearing through Bidur, a town about 50 kilometers (31 miles) northwest of Nepal’s capital Kathmandu, bursting the banks of a river, causing multi-storey buildings to collapse and washing away a bridge.

How many people have been killed?

At least 95 people have been killed, police in Nepal’s Bagmati province said earlier today, but that is not a true indicator of the destruction. Almost 400 travelers, including hundreds of foreign nationals, have been reported missing in Nepal, the country’s tourism board said. Italy’s foreign ministry say 90 Italians in the area are missing. And 60 employees of an under-construction hydropower project in northern Nepal are also missing, according to Nepali state media.

Three people have been killed in Tibet and 265 others are missing, Chinese authorities said earlier today.

What rescue efforts are happening?

Rescue helicopters are struggling to land in the affected areas because the floodwaters are so high, Nepali authorities said earlier today, according to Reuters. However, the Nepali army posted videos of helicopters hovering just above the floodwater and buildings, so that people could clamber to safety.

China has mobilized multiple agencies to respond to the disaster in Tibet, with Chinese state media saying the top leadership quickly guided the response to the disaster, suggesting the potential severity of impact.
